q: Statement I: The college's water pump broke down on Monday morning. Statement II: Hostel students could not get water for bathing on Monday. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Both statements are effects of independent causes
x: With the pump broken, water could not reach the hostel. The breakdown came first and produced the shortage.

q: Statement I: Onion prices in the markets rose sharply. Statement II: Floods destroyed a large part of the onion crop. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Both statements are effects of independent causes
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
x: Losing much of the crop cuts the supply of onions, which pushes prices up. The flood damage is the cause, even though it is written second.

q: Statement I: Many flights at Islamabad airport were delayed on Tuesday morning because pilots could not see the runway clearly. Statement II: Traffic on the motorway near Islamabad moved very slowly on Tuesday morning because drivers could hardly see the road. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
x: Flight delays do not slow motorway traffic, nor the other way round. Both statements point to the same poor visibility that morning, such as thick fog, so they are effects of a common cause.

q: Statement I: The college canteen ran out of food by noon. Statement II: The canteen's supplier did not deliver that morning. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Both statements are effects of independent causes
x: Without the morning delivery, the canteen had too little food for the day. The missed delivery caused the shortage.

q: Statement I: A new mobile phone model went on sale in Karachi. Statement II: The wheat harvest in Punjab was good this year. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Both statements are effects of independent causes
x: A phone launch and a good harvest have no link with each other and no shared cause. Each has its own separate reason.

q: Statement I: Many people in the city suffered from heatstroke last week. Statement II: Demand for electricity in the city reached a record high last week. Which of the following is correct?
o: Both statements are effects of some common cause
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
x: Heatstroke does not raise electricity demand, and demand does not cause heatstroke. A severe heatwave would explain both.

q: Ali's phone battery lasted a full day when the phone was new, but two years later it runs out in a few hours, though he uses the phone in the same way. What is the most likely cause?
o: The phone's screen has become larger
The battery has aged and now holds less charge
Ali's SIM card has expired
The phone's camera has been damaged
x: Rechargeable batteries slowly lose capacity with age and use. Since his use has not changed, an ageing battery best explains the shorter life.

q: An iron gate in a coastal town rusts much faster than an identical gate in a dry inland town. What is the most likely cause?
o: The coastal gate is opened less often
The moist, salty air near the sea speeds up rusting
Inland gates are painted every week by law
Iron does not rust in dry towns at all
x: Rusting needs water and oxygen, and salt speeds it up. Coastal air has more moisture and salt, so the gate there rusts faster.

q: A car would not start on a cold morning. Its headlights did not come on and its horn made no sound. What is the most likely cause?
o: The fuel tank was empty
One of the tyres was flat
The car's battery was flat
The engine oil was old
x: The starter, lights and horn all run on the battery, so one flat battery explains all three. An empty fuel tank would not stop the lights or horn working.

q: In a garden, plants placed in the shade of a high wall grew poorly, while the same kind of plants in the open, given the same soil and water, grew well. What is the most likely cause?
o: The wall made the soil more fertile
The plants in the wall's shade received less sunlight
The open plants were given more water
Plants cannot grow near any wall
x: Soil and water were the same, so the difference lies in light. Plants need sunlight to make food, and the wall's shade reduced it.

q: Statement I: Far more people than usual visited the city's parks on Sunday. Statement II: Sunday was a pleasant, sunny day after a week of rain. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Both statements are effects of independent causes
x: Fine weather after days of rain encourages people to go out. The weather is the cause of the larger crowds, even though it is stated second.

q: Statement I: An oil tanker ship leaked oil near the coast. Statement II: Many sea birds near the coast were found covered in oil. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Both statements are effects of independent causes
x: The leaked oil spread over the water and coated the birds. The leak came first and caused the harm.

q: Some people believe that a black cat crossing the road brings bad luck. Which is a valid argument against this belief?
o: A cat's path has no possible link to later events, and there is no evidence of such an effect
Many people in the town believe it
Black cats are rarer than other cats
Cats cross roads mostly at night
x: A belief needs a link between cause and effect and evidence to support it. Popularity or how often cats cross roads proves nothing.

q: A student believes that sleeping with a book under his pillow will help him remember what is in it. Which is a valid argument against this belief?
o: Pillows are too soft to hold books
Memory depends on studying and revising; a book under the pillow cannot pass information into the brain
Some books are too thick to put under a pillow
Other students also keep books under their pillows
x: Learning comes from reading and practice. Having a book nearby while asleep gives the brain no information to store.

q: Some people believe that cold weather on its own gives people the flu. Which is a valid argument against this belief?
o: Flu is more common in summer than in winter
Cold weather makes people stay indoors and sleep
Flu is caused by a virus, so a person catches it only after being exposed to the virus
Many people enjoy cold weather
x: Influenza is an infection caused by a virus. Cold weather alone cannot cause it without the virus being passed on.

q: Hira says her plant grew faster this month because she talked kindly to it every morning. During the same month, she had moved it to a much sunnier window. Which is the most valid conclusion?
o: The move to more sunlight is a known cause of faster growth and could explain the change
Talking to the plant must be the only reason for its growth
The plant would have died if she had stopped talking
Plants grow faster only when people are near them
x: Plants need light to make food, so more sunlight can explain faster growth. Because two things changed at once, the talking cannot be proved to be the cause.

q: A man says, "Vaccines make children ill, because my nephew had a mild fever the day after his vaccination." Which is a valid argument against his claim?
o: A short mild fever can be a normal reaction, and one case cannot outweigh large studies showing vaccines prevent disease
His nephew is too young to have a fever
Fevers happen only in winter
Doctors never give more than one vaccine
x: A brief mild fever is a known, usually harmless reaction to some vaccines. One case cannot overturn evidence from large studies that vaccines protect against disease.

q: Hamza believes that if someone sneezes as he leaves the house, his journey will go badly. Which is a valid reason to reject this belief?
o: A sneeze is a body reflex to irritation in the nose and cannot affect events on a journey
People sneeze more often in spring
Hamza does not travel very often
Sneezing is more common in crowded places
x: A sneeze has a physical cause inside the body. Nothing links it to what happens later on a journey.

q: In a town, people who own more books tend to live longer. Someone concludes that owning books makes people live longer. Which fact, if true, best shows the flaw in this conclusion?
o: Books are sold in many shops in the town
Some people borrow books from the library
Reading can be done at any age
Wealthier families both buy more books and can afford better health care
x: Wealth could cause both more books and longer lives, so the books need not be the cause. A third factor can create a link between two things.

q: People in a village believe that eating fish and then drinking milk causes white patches on the skin. Which is a valid argument against this belief?
o: Fish and milk are both expensive
Milk is drunk mostly at breakfast
White patches result from loss of the skin's pigment cells, and no study has linked them to eating fish with milk
Many people in the village believe it
x: The patches are due to loss of pigment-making cells in the skin. With no evidence of any link to the food, the belief should be rejected.

q: Sana revised for only one day before her exam. On the way to the exam she saw a crow, and later she blamed the crow for her poor result. What is the valid explanation of her result?
o: The crow brought her bad luck
Too little revision, not the crow, explains her poor result
Exams are always harder on days when crows are seen
Her result was decided before she sat the exam
x: Preparation affects exam marks directly, and she did very little. A bird seen on the way has no link to her answers.

q: Which belief can be rejected because there is no possible cause-and-effect link?
o: Covering food keeps flies away from it
Washing fruit removes some dirt and germs
Wearing a seat belt reduces injury in a crash
Hanging a lemon and chillies at a shop door keeps losses away
x: Lemons and chillies have no way of affecting a shop's business. The other three describe real causes and effects.

q: Rashid claims that a full moon makes people behave more aggressively, because the emergency ward was very busy on the last full-moon night. What is the best way to test his claim?
o: Ask Rashid how strongly he believes it
Check whether the moon was bright on that one night
Compare emergency records over many full-moon nights with many other nights
Count how many people looked at the moon that night
x: One busy night proves nothing. Comparing many full-moon nights with many ordinary nights would show whether any real difference exists.

q: Usman scored poorly in his first mock test and says, "I am not smart enough to become a doctor." Which argument most strongly challenges his belief?
o: Mock tests are always easier than the real exam
One mock test shows what he needs to work on, and many students raise their scores through regular practice
He should stop taking mock tests
Becoming a doctor depends only on luck
x: A single low score is feedback, not proof of ability. Steady practice usually improves results, so his conclusion goes far beyond the evidence.

q: Statement I: A village started classes to teach adults to read. Statement II: More villagers began reading the health leaflets given out at the local clinic. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Both statements are effects of independent causes
x: Learning to read made it possible for adults to use the leaflets. The classes came first and caused the change.

q: Statement I: The number of road accidents on a highway fell this year. Statement II: Speed cameras were installed along the highway last year. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Both statements are effects of independent causes
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
x: Speed cameras make drivers slow down, which lowers accidents. The cameras came first and are the cause, even though they are stated second.

q: Statement: Should students keep a daily study timetable? Argument I: Yes, a timetable helps students cover all subjects and use their time well. Argument II: No, making a timetable is boring. Which argument is strong?
o: Only argument II is strong
Both arguments I and II are strong
Only argument I is strong
Neither argument I nor II is strong
x: Argument I gives a real benefit linked to the question. Finding a task boring is not a strong reason against doing it.

q: Statement I: Students cleared the garbage from their street. Statement II: Fewer flies and mosquitoes were seen in the street afterwards. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
x: Garbage provides breeding places and food for flies and mosquitoes. Removing it led to fewer insects.

q: After an operation, Fatima feels she will never walk normally again. Her doctor says most patients with her operation walk normally again after regular physiotherapy. Which conclusion is both logical and positive?
o: She will certainly never walk again
She will walk normally even without physiotherapy
Physiotherapy is useful only for athletes
By doing regular physiotherapy as advised, she has a good chance of walking normally again
x: The doctor's information shows that most such patients recover with physiotherapy. Her chance is good if she follows the advice, so hopeless fear is not justified.

q: Statement I: More girls from a district joined medical colleges this year. Statement II: Two years ago, a free science coaching centre for girls opened in the district. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Both statements are effects of independent causes
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
x: The coaching began two years earlier, giving students time to prepare. Better preparation then led to more admissions, so the centre is the cause.

q: A shopkeeper's shop was badly damaged in a flood. He says, "Everything is lost; there is no point in starting again." Which is the strongest argument to encourage him?
o: Floods never happen twice in the same place
He should wait for his luck to change by itself
He still has his skills and his customers' trust, which he can use to rebuild step by step
Other shopkeepers lost even more than he did
x: His skills and reputation are real resources that make rebuilding possible. The other replies rely on false claims, luck or comparison rather than a reason to act.

q: Statement I: A hospital in Peshawar held a free eye camp. Statement II: A college in Lahore won a national debating competition. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Both statements are effects of independent causes
x: The eye camp and the debate win are unrelated events in different cities. Neither causes the other, and they share no common cause.

q: Statement I: Most students in a college improved their biology marks this term after a new biology teacher joined. Statement II: Most students in the same college improved their chemistry marks this term after the chemistry laboratory was fully re-equipped. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
x: Better biology marks do not cause better chemistry marks, or the reverse. Each improvement follows its own separate cause (a new teacher, a re-equipped laboratory), so they are effects of independent causes.

q: Statement: Should hospitals hold free health-check camps in villages? Argument I: Yes, they help find diseases early when treatment is easier. Argument II: No, villagers can travel to cities whenever they wish. Which argument is strong?
o: Only argument II is strong
Both arguments I and II are strong
Only argument I is strong
Neither argument I nor II is strong
x: Early detection is a real and important benefit. Argument II is weak because many villagers cannot easily travel to cities for check-ups.
